1	# AI Logs
2	
3	This folder holds every AI session for each sprint, one folder per student. The course rules are on
4	the [AI Log Instructions](https://csci-435-se.github.io/ai-logs/) page and the current sprint page
5	at <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>. This README is the team's shared convention for following them.
6	
7	## What to log
8	
9	Every AI session tied to this project: code, debugging, tests, reviews, drafting issues and PRs,
10	design discussion, the sprint report. That includes sessions that went nowhere. Purely academic
11	questions unrelated to the project don't need logging.
12	
13	## Structure
14	
15	```
16	ai-logs/
17	  sprint1/
18	    <github-username>/                          ← exact GitHub username, matching case
19	      .gitkeep                                  ← the folder must exist even if you used no AI
20	      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md
21	      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>/           ← attachments (images, etc.), optional
22	```
23	
24	Team folders: `ab-wm`, `arjunsb26`, `CarsonRackley`, `controlled-opposition`, `Jack-Donohue`,
25	`vvchopra`.
26	
27	## Naming
28	
29	`YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`
30	
31	- **Date:** the day the session started.
32	- **Sprint folder:** the sprint that date falls in, not the sprint the work is for.
33	- **Tool:** one of the course identifiers: `claude-code`, `claude-web`, `claude-desktop`, `cursor`,
34	  `gemini-cli`, `codex-cli`, `copilot`, `chatgpt`, `other-<name>`. Claude Code run inside VS Code is
35	  `claude-code`.
36	- **Slug:** lowercase words joined with hyphens that say what the session did. Put the issue number
37	  first when there is one: `issue-52-impl`, `issue-52-spec`, `pr-61-review`, `sprint1-report`.
38	  Replace auto-generated slugs such as `local-command-caveat...`.
39	- **Formats:** `.md` is preferred; `.txt` and `.json` are also accepted. No `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.html`
40	  or share links.
41	
42	## Capturing a session
43	
44	| Tool | How |
45	| --- | --- |
46	| Claude Code (terminal or VS Code), other agentic CLIs | Start it with [SpecStory](https://specstory.com/): `specstory run claude`, from the repo root. Forgot? Run `specstory sync` afterwards; it back-fills from Claude Code's local history. Then copy from `.specstory/history/` (git-ignored) into your folder and rename it to the convention. |
47	| Web chat (claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini, ...) | Install a browser chat exporter and export the session as Markdown right after it ends. Include any files you pasted in as context. |
48	| Claude Desktop | SpecStory doesn't capture it. Copy the conversation into a `.md` file by hand. |
49	
50	At the end of each sprint, run `specstory sync` once more and re-copy. A log copied mid-session is
51	incomplete.
52	
53	## Content
54	
55	- The **tool and AI model** used (SpecStory writes both).
56	- The **complete** prompt and response history. For agentic tools, that includes file edits and
57	  commands (SpecStory includes them). Logs with missing responses or truncated histories are
58	  **invalid**. Don't hand-write, summarise or trim a log; only rename it.
59	- Attachments (screenshots, snippets) go in a folder with the log's name minus `.md`.
60	- Log **every** session, including ones that went nowhere. Grading is on how complete the record
61	  is, not on whether AI helped.
62	
63	## Where logs are referenced
64	
65	- **Issue comments only.** Each contributor posts their own `### AI Assistance — @username` comment
66	  on the issue, with full `https://github.com/...` links to their logs. Format:
67	  [`.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md`](../.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md).
68	- **Not** in PR descriptions or PR comments. The PR has a short AI-use note with no log link. The
69	  AI Log Instructions page says "Issue/PR comments", but the Sprint 1 page narrows this to issue
70	  comments only, and the sprint page wins.
71	- Each teammate posts their own comment, including reviewers who used AI to review.
72	- No AI used? Post an issue comment saying so, and keep your folder with its `.gitkeep`.
73	- The sprint report lists each member's tools, session count, folder link, and 2–3 sentences on
74	  lessons learned.
75
```

# Risks and Retrospective 

- Windows development environments: native Windows produced false test failures and extremely slow linting, and Go had to be pinned to 1.26.4 because Go 1.27 reformats existing files. Several members spent significant time setting up WSL.  
- Shared CI failures: a lint error in \`STUDENTS.md\` on \`main\` failed CI for every open PR until \#15 was merged, which showed how one broken file on \`main\` blocks the whole team.  
- Codebase size: Gitea has about 40 service packages, 85 module packages, and more than 300 migrations,  so concept location takes much longer than expected. Furthermore, changes are more difficult to make as there are far too many interactions between different components of the project.  
- Overlapping PRs: PRs \#8, \#9, and \#15 contained the same files, which inflated diffs and forced a specific merge order.  
- Review bottleneck: one required approval with only a f[TRUNCATED]

1:# Course workflow — issues, PRs, reviews, sprint deliverables
2-
3-Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>
4-(Sprints pages) and `docs/sprint0/standards.md`. Everyone on the team, and every AI session, uses
5-the formats below so all issues and PRs look the same. The GitHub templates in `.github/` carry the
6-same formats; if they ever disagree with this page, fix the template.
7-
8-AI disclosure has its own page: `AI-ASSISTANCE.md`.
9-
10-## Current sprint: Sprint 1
11-
12-- **Dates:** Sep 22 – Oct 8, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Oct 8, 11:59 PM**.
13-- **Points:** 100 (10% of the course grade).
14-- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D6) or no release (D7) means **0 for the
15-  whole sprint**.
16-- **Carries forward:** every Sprint 0 standard and convention still applies.
17-
18-| # | Deliverable | Points | Who | Where |
19-| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
20-| D1 | Sprint backlog: a `Sprint 1` milestone with every selected issue on it | 10 | Team | GitHub milestone |
21:| D2 | Requirements spec for each issue (formats below), peer-reviewed by a teammate | 20 | Individual | Issue body |
22-| D3 | At least one non-trivial design decision per issue | 7 | Individual | Issue body |
23-| D4 | Code changes and PRs | 36 | Individual | PRs |
24-| D5 | AI logs | 7 | Individual | `ai-logs/sprint1/<github-username>/` |
25-| D6 | Sprint report | 10 | Team | `docs/sprint1/report.md` |
26-| D7 | Release: tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s1` plus a GitHub release | 2 | Team | Tags / Releases |
27-| D8 | Reflection survey | 8 | Individual | Blackboard/Zulip link |
28-
29-- **D1 load:** each CSCI 435 student owns at least 2 medium issues; each CSCI 535 student owns at
30-  least 2 medium and 1 small. Every issue has exactly **one** assignee. Specs should be final by
31-  Sep 27.
32-- **D5:** conventions are in `ai-logs/README.md`. The folder must exist even if no AI was used. In
33-  that case, post an issue comment saying so. Log links go in **issue comments only**, never in PRs
34-  (`AI-ASSISTANCE.md`).
35-- **D7:** keep Sprint 0's base version (`v1.27.3-csci435-s0` → `v1.27.3-csci435-s1`), push the tag
36-  to origin, and write release notes listing the features, fixes and improvements.
37:- **Reviews:** each student reviews at least one PR per sprint. Over the semester, each student
38:  reviews every teammate at least once.
39-- **Extra credit:** up to 3 points per PR accepted by upstream Gitea.
40-

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any
   change that can't be tested automatically and how it was checked by hand. Every behaviour change
   needs a new or updated test.
5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status, or the commands run and their results.
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6, test strategy with
explanation 5, description quality 4, CI or manual verification 3, review rubric posted 2.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.

```markdown
### Code Review — @reviewer-username

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

## Sprint report (D6) sections

`docs/sprint<N>/report.md`, following `docs/sprint0/report.md`:

- Team: names, GitHub usernames, project name, repository link.
- Sprint overview.
- Backlog: milestone link, plus a table of title, owner, points, scope and status.
- Requirements and design: when specs were done, what surprised you, design rationale.
- Completed issues: title, owner, PR link, author, reviewer, what changed.
- Test strategy, including untestable changes and why.
- AI tool usage per member: tools, session count, AI log folder link, and 2–3 sentences on lessons
  learned.
- Release: tag and release link.
- Risks and retrospective: what worked, what slowed the team down, Sprint 2 changes.
- Sprint 2 plan: initial ideas and carryover issues.
======ISSUE
Accessible names for icon-only dropdown triggers
> Sub-issue of #25 · **P1** · estimate **2 points** (small) · blocked by nothing

## User Story
As a screen reader user, I want every dropdown trigger to announce what it does, so that I am not
told only "menu, collapsed" and left to open it to find out what it was.

## User Scenario
A user Tabs through an issue thread. On each comment they reach the "..." button. Today the reader
announces nothing useful — the button's only content is an SVG. After this change it announces
"Comment options, menu, collapsed", so they can skip past it or open it deliberately.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a dropdown whose trigger contains only an icon, when the page is initialised,
      then the trigger has a non-empty accessible name.
- [ ] AC2: Given the comment context menu in
      `templates/repo/issue/view_content/context_menu.tmpl`, which today has neither `aria-label`
      nor `data-tooltip-content`, then its trigger announces a localised name.
- [ ] AC3: Given the footer theme selector `#footer-theme-selector` in
      `templates/base/footer_content.tmpl`, then its trigger announces a localised name.
- [ ] AC4: Given a dropdown that already has an `aria-label`, then this change does not overwrite
      it; given one with only a `data-tooltip-content`, then the existing fallback in
      `attachStaticElements` still applies.
- [ ] AC5: Given a development build, when a dropdown is initialised with no accessible name from
      any source, then a console warning names the element, so the next one is caught before
      review; no warning is emitted in production builds.
- [ ] AC6: Unit tests in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.test.ts` cover AC1, AC4 and AC5.

## Out of Scope
- Adding names to anything that is not a dropdown trigger — buttons, links and icon-only form
  controls elsewhere have the same problem and deserve their own issue.
- Changing how any dropdown behaves.
- The dropdowns migrated in #62, which get their names from the new component's own markup.

## Open Questions
- How many of the 61 `ui dropdown` occurrences are actually icon-only? The audit in this issue
  produces that number; if it is much larger than expected, split the template fixes into a
  follow-up and keep the fallback plus the warning here.

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Add the missing `aria-label` attributes in the templates, and add a dev-only warning
in `dropdown.ts` for any dropdown left without a name — rather than synthesising a name in JS.

**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Derive a name in JS from the dropdown's icon, for example from
the `octicon-kebab-horizontal` class. (b) Add a generic fallback such as "Menu" in JS for any
unnamed dropdown.

**Rationale:** (a) produces names derived from the picture rather than the purpose — the same
kebab icon is "comment options" in one place and something else elsewhere — and the icon name is
not translatable. (b) silences the screen reader problem without solving it: "Menu, collapsed" is
barely better than nothing, and it would permanently hide the missing names from the AC5 warning.
Putting the name in the template keeps it next to the thing it describes and in the locale system,
and the warning makes the remaining gaps visible instead of papering over them.

**Consequences:** Easier — names are localised, accurate, and each one is reviewable in context;
new unnamed dropdowns get caught in development. Harder — every new icon-only dropdown needs an
explicit `aria-label` and there is no safety net at runtime, so a missed one is silent in
production; the AC5 warning only helps contributors who run a dev build and read the console.

## Scope
small (2 points)

+// role=menu takes no name from its content, but a trigger with visible text is at least not icon-only
+function hasAccessibleName(dropdown: HTMLElement, focusable: HTMLElement): boolean {
+  for (const el of [dropdown, focusable]) {
+    if (['aria-label', 'aria-labelledby', 'title', 'placeholder'].some((attr) => el.getAttribute(attr))) return true;
+  }
+  if ((focusable as HTMLInputElement).labels?.length) return true; // a search input with <label for>
+  for (const node of dropdown.childNodes) {
+    if (node.nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE && node.textContent!.trim()) return true;
+    if (!(node instanceof Element) || node.matches('.menu, select')) continue; // popup items and a wrapped <select>'s options are not the trigger
+    if (node.textContent.trim() || node.matches('img[alt]:not([alt=""])') || node.querySelector('img[alt]:not([alt=""])')) return true;

name: gitea-wsync-test-workflow
description: Edit code in this Windows Gitea folder; run tests/lint/build in WSL Debian ~/gitea via `wsync <cmd>` from Git Bash
metadata:
  type: project
---
Carson's setup (2026-09-14): **all code edits happen in this Windows `Gitea` folder** (logged
SpecStory sessions launch here). WSL Debian `~/gitea` is a **test runner only** — never edit there.
Native Windows test runs produce Windows-only failures, and lint is ~20x slower, so don't trust them.
**Run tests/lint/build with `wsync` from the Bash tool (Git Bash):**
```bash
wsync pnpm exec vitest run web_src/js/features/common-page.test.ts
wsync go test -run '^TestName$' ./routers/web/misc/
wsync make lint-js
wsync make build
wsync            # sync only
```
`C:\Users\carso\bin\wsync` reads the branch checked out here, warns if tracked files are
uncommitted (only COMMITTED work reaches WSL — commit first, ask Carson before committing), then
runs WSL `~/bin/wsync-wsl <branch> [cmd]`: fetches remote `win` (this folder over /mnt/c;
push disabled), force-switches `~/gitea` to that branch, runs the command with Go 1.26.4/Node PATH.
Gotchas: don't run `git status` on `/mnt/c` from WSL (hangs); WSL can't run `.exe`s; use
`wsl -d Debian --exec bash -c '...' name args` (plain `wsl -- bash -c` drops args).
To try the app: `~/gitea/custom/conf/app.ini` serves Gitea on http://localhost:3001 (SQLite) —
run `wsl -d Debian --exec bash -c 'cd ~/gitea && ./gitea web'` in the background after `wsync make build`.
Baseline rule: some backend tests fail on `main` too — compare branch vs `main`, not vs zero.

name: gitea-toolchain-setup
description: Toolchain for the CSCI 435 Gitea project — pinned Go version, make-from-Git-Bash rule, stale corepack step
metadata:
  type: project
---
Installed 2026-09-02 for [[csci-435-gitea-project]]: **Go 1.26.4**, Node 26.7.0, corepack 0.36.0,
pnpm 11.9.0, GNU Make 4.4.1 (ezwinports, at
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WinGet\Packages\ezwinports.make_*\bin`). No gcc needed (pure-Go SQLite,
`CGO_ENABLED=0`). Verified: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `vite build`, `go build` (~149 MB
`gitea.exe`), and `make fmt` all exit 0 with a clean tree.
**Go must stay on 1.26.x — do not upgrade to 1.27.** `go.mod` says `go 1.26.4` and CI resolves from
it (`go-version-file: go.mod`). Go 1.27's gofmt reformats multi-value composite-literal returns, so
`make fmt` under 1.27 rewrites `modules/git/key.go` and drags unrelated churn into PRs. Confirmed by
testing both versions. The winget package is **pinned** (`winget pin add --id GoLang.Go`), so
`winget upgrade --all` skips it; `winget pin remove --id GoLang.Go` if the course bumps `go.mod`.
**Run `make` from Git Bash, never PowerShell.** PowerShell has no POSIX `sh` on PATH, so make falls
back to `cmd.exe` and dies with `'sed' is not recognized`. Do NOT "fix" this by adding Git's
`usr\bin` to the global PATH — it shadows Windows `find`/`sort`.
**`STUDENTS.md` is stale on pnpm:** it says `corepack enable`, but Node 25+ unbundled corepack, so
that fails on Node 26. Fix used: `npm install -g corepack@latest`, then `corepack enable pnpm` and
`corepack prepare pnpm@11.9.0 --activate`. npm's global prefix is user-writable (no admin), but Go
and Node MSIs raise UAC prompts Claude cannot click — Carson must approve those.
Tests: do not run on native Windows (`STUDENTS.md` — symlink/temp-file failures that aren't real
bugs). WSL2 Debian is now set up — run tests via `wsync <cmd>`, see [[gitea-wsync-test-workflow]].

# AI assistance disclosure — required format

Course rule, not an upstream Gitea one. Every contributor discloses their own AI use per issue,
**even when no AI was used**. Source: the course AI Log Instructions page and `CONTRIBUTING.md`
(AI Contribution Policy). Two separate places, both required. The rest of the PR and issue
format is in `COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.

## 1. A comment on the issue

Posted by each contributor on the **issue** they worked, once their work is done. One comment per
person — never edit someone else's. Add later sessions by editing your own table.

```markdown
### AI Assistance — @your-github-username

**Role in this issue:** Implementation

| # | Tool | Log | What AI helped with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | claude-code | [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/blob/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md) | Confirmed the files found during concept location, drafted the template change and tests, ran them |

**Attachments:** [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl/](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/tree/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl)
```

- **Role** is one of Implementation, Code review, Testing, Other — pick the ones that apply and
  delete the rest, do not leave the slash list in place.
- **Tool** is the tool's name, e.g. `claude-code`, `claude-web`.
- **Log** is a full `https://github.com/...` link to the filed log. Relative paths break in issue
  comments. File naming is in `ai-logs/README.md`.
- **Attachments** only when the log has a companion folder; otherwise drop the line.
- **No AI used?** Keep the heading and role line and write `No AI used` in place of the table.

## 2. A short section in the pull request description — no log link

Reviewers read the PR, and the review rubric scores "AI transparency", so the PR says how AI was
used and how you verified it. It does **not** link or cite the AI log: from Sprint 1 on, logs are
referenced in **issue comments only**, never in PR descriptions or PR comments (Sprint 1 page, D5).

```markdown
## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5) drafted the handler and tests following the existing register/delete
code; I reviewed every line, ran the tests, checked the page by hand, and can explain each change.
AI log: see the AI Assistance comment on the linked issue.
```

Name the model, say what AI did and what you did, and point at the issue comment for the log.

## Rules that make a disclosure wrong

- **Placeholders left in**: `@your-github-username` or the full `Implementation / Code review /
  Testing / Other` list means the comment was pasted unread.
- **A log link in a PR description or PR comment.** Log links live in the issue comment only.
- **A log link that 404s.** Until the log is merged to `main`, link the branch that holds it; switch
  to the `main` link once merged.
- **A log folder that is not your GitHub username** — `ai-logs/sprint1/jdonohue/` is wrong when the
  account is `Jack-Donohue`.
- **Claiming work AI did as your own, or the reverse.** The claim must match the log.
- **AI-written replies to reviewer questions on your own issue or PR.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` forbids it:
  the questions are for you.

## For AI agents drafting an issue or PR

Put section 2 in every PR description you draft, and draft the section 1 issue comment
separately, both filled in from the session you actually ran — never with placeholders. You may
draft the wording, but say plainly that the human must review and edit it before posting, and leave
the issue comment for them to post under their own account.

15	### What we planned to do
16	
17	At the start of the sprint, we were hit with the problem that most issues were ambitious and large in scope, making it difficult to cleanly assign work between different members of the team.
18	
19	A number of large issues, namely #7, #12, #23 and #25, were cut down into smaller medium and small issues that were easier to manage. The plan was to complete these large issues, with members who split the issues into smaller issues working on the backbone of the problem, and then distributing the issues among other members to complete them.
20	
21	### Scope Changes
22	
23	While we certainly got close to completing all of the aforementioned large issues, and managed to complete all 13 issues in the Sprint 1 milestone (#12 through its sub-issues #53, #54 and #55, plus #50, #51, #61, #62, #63, #64, #14, #34 and #35), larger than expected issues and requests from product owners made it difficult to achieve our goal. The request from the product owner to complete #14, or “Add a burndown chart to milestones with an ideal line and projected finish,” was one of the main reasons we had to change the scope of this sprint.
24	
25	Issue #14 was a large issue, and with one of our team members completely devoted to this purpose, we had to change the scope of the sprint to ensure we are able to complete the main issues, and leave cleanup work for the next sprint. Because of this, #64 was only picked up on the last day of the sprint (PR #81), the keyboard shortcut issues (#56, #57) were deferred and moved out of the milestone, and #52 was moved to Sprint 2.
26	
27	Fortunately, however, we were able to complete #12 and #14 in full, along with the core of #7 and #25 (#50, #51 and #61–#64), so we still consider this sprint to be a success. The remaining sub-issues (#52, #65 and #56–#60) carry over into Sprint 2.

57	## Requirements & Design
58	
59	Were specs complete before coding started? Any surprises? Key design decisions and brief rationale
60	
61	### State of issues at the start of the sprint
62	
63	Most of the issues carried over from Sprint 0 (#7, #12, #14, #23, #25, #34, #35) were written as summaries or proposals, not in the Sprint 1 spec format. Each owner rewrote their issue into a User Story, User Scenario, numbered Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope and Open Questions, and a teammate posted a "Spec Reviewed" comment on the issue before implementation started.
64	
65	Surprises:
66	
67	- #35 was sent back ("Spec Reviewed: Not yet") for numbered acceptance criteria and was approved after it was revised.
68	- #14's spec was refined late, after implementation had already started.
69	- The review of #64 found that one of its acceptance criteria was already met by #62.
70	- Close reasons (#12) needed a database change and reached into automatic closes (commits, cross-references and the API), which became its own sub-issue (#55).
71	
72	### Key decisions that led to the splitting of Issues
73	
74	- **#7 Overhauled notifications system** → #50 (filter), #51 (bulk actions), #52 (sort). #52 was moved to Sprint 2 because it needs a database migration and a queue change.
75	- **#12 Close reasons** → #53 (storage and backend), #54 (UI), #55 (automatic and API closes). The issue was split by layer so that the backend could be merged first and the UI could build on it.
76	- **#25 Make dropdowns Accessible** → #61 (menu web component), #62 (menu migration), #63 (multi-select ARIA), #64 (icon-only triggers), #65 (Playwright regression suite). #61 had to be merged before #62 could use it.
77	- **#23 Keyboard navigation/shortcuts** → #56–#60, all deferred to keep the sprint scope achievable.
78	- **#14, #34 and #35** were kept as single issues. #14 is large and counts as two medium issues.
79	
80	### Key design decisions
81	
82	- **#50:** "Mark all as read" respects the active filter.
83	- **#51:** "Select all" only selects the notifications in the current view, with an explicit "Select all N notifications in this view" link. Bulk actions never reach outside the active view.
84	- **#53:** `CloseIssue` becomes a wrapper over a new `CloseIssueWithReason`, so existing callers keep working unchanged.
85	- **#54:** Picking "Duplicate" or "Other" opens a small popup under the close button, and each close reason gets its own icon.
86	- **#55:** Automatic closes record a default reason (completed for issues, not planned for pull requests).
87	- **#61:** The menu is built as a custom element under `web_src/js/webcomponents/`, without Fomantic.
88	- **#62:** Only static, server-rendered, single-select menus are migrated.
89	- **#63:** The existing Fomantic dropdown patch is extended rather than replaced.
90	- **#34:** `?due=` is parsed once into deadline bounds that both the database search and the issue indexer use.
91	- **#35:** A member or outside collaborator without two-factor authentication is treated as a non-member of the organization until they enrol. This is a reversible lockout: nothing is deleted.
92	- **#14:** Each milestone's history is rebuilt when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and served from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders, instead of a daily snapshot table that would have no history for existing milestones.

199	
200	## Risks and Retrospective
201	
202	What worked:
203	
204	- Splitting the large issues into sub-issues gave each member at least two medium issues and let work happen in parallel.
205	- The "Spec Reviewed" step caught gaps before coding started (#35 was revised before it was approved).
206	- Writing tests per acceptance criterion, and checking the tests by deliberately breaking code (#67, #68), produced well-specified PRs.
207	- CodeRabbit, added mid-sprint, gave quick first-pass reviews on #71–#77, alongside the required human rubric reviews.
208	
209	What slowed the team:
210	
211	- Review bottleneck: most PRs were opened in the last three days of the sprint (#71–#81, Oct 6–8), and one required approval with only a few active reviewers slowed merging. Four PRs (#73, #76, #77, #81) were merged in the final hours, and #81 was opened on the last evening.
212	- #77's burndown test passes on SQLite, MySQL and MSSQL but fails on PostgreSQL in CI, because events in the same second come back in a different order. It was merged on the last day with that check still failing, and the fix carries over into Sprint 2.
213	- #14 was a large issue that took one member the whole sprint, and its spec was refined late.
214	- Open PRs fell 25 commits behind `main` as other PRs merged and had to be updated.
215	- AI logs committed inside feature PRs made the diffs 16,000–32,000 lines long, which made them harder to review.
216	- CodeRabbit's autofix pushed a commit directly to a teammate's branch (#76).
217	- Codebase size: Gitea has about 40 service packages, 85 module packages, and more than 300 migrations, so concept location still takes much longer than expected.
218	
219	Changes for Sprint 2:
220	
221	- Open PRs by the middle of the sprint and request a reviewer when opening them, aiming for a review within 24 hours.
222	- Don't start a branch until the spec is "Approved".
223	- Commit AI logs in a separate chore PR, as #78 did.
224	- Use CodeRabbit as a first pass only, with no autofix on someone else's branch without the author's OK.
225	- Update the branch from `main` before requesting a review.
226	
227	## Sprint 2 Plan
228	
229	Brief ideas on the features the team intends to tackle; any setup still needed
230	
231	We plan to fix #77's failing PostgreSQL burndown test first, then address #52 (sort notifications by reason or type, spec already posted), #65 (Playwright keyboard regression suite for dropdowns) and the keyboard shortcut issues under #23 (#56–#60) first, along with two small follow-ups from the #81 review (the merge-style button in the pull request merge box and the repository topics editor still have no accessible name), split between 2-3 members between each. This will not be a strict split, though it should help complete issues faster, akin to pair programming under the extreme programming paradigm.
232	
233	If we complete these issues quicker than the end of the sprint, we will attempt to implement more medium term issues to the extent possible.
